lessons.title: Music, water and an argument

n1.text: Two young men in fine clothes sit on the grass making music. Two women without clothes are with them. Nobody looks surprised.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Count the people first. Then find the one who is far away, and listen for the sounds in the picture.

q1.text: What is the standing woman on the left doing?

b1a.text: The pipe belongs to the seated woman.

correction.truth: The seated woman holds the pipe. The standing woman pours water from a glass jug into a stone basin.
correction.evidence: The photo; Walter Pater (1893); the Louvre.

b1b.text: Yes. She tips a glass jug over a stone basin. Water and music: the sound of pouring joins the lute and the pipe.

b1c.text: Her hands hold a jug, not fruit.

correction.tempting: She stands under a tree, reaching out.
correction.truth: She is pouring water from a glass jug into a stone basin.
correction.evidence: The photo; Walter Pater (1893); the Louvre.

n2.text: For a long time this picture was called a Giorgione. Louis XIV's inventory of 1683 names him, and so do writers around 1900.

q2.text: Whose name does the Louvre's label give today?

b2a.text: His name came first, but not today.

correction.tempting: The king's inventory of 1683 says Giorgione.
correction.truth: The Louvre now gives it to Titian, after centuries of argument about who painted it.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; the National Gallery, London.

b2b.text: An old guess, long given up.

correction.tempting: Critics of the 1800s gave it to an imitator of Sebastiano.
correction.truth: The Louvre now gives it to Titian, after centuries of argument.
correction.evidence: Walter Pater (1893); the Louvre; the National Gallery, London.

b2c.text: Yes, Titian. But it was long called Giorgione's, and who painted it has been argued over for centuries. The label keeps both names.

n3.text: Titian learned from Giorgione and worked with him. Giorgione died of the plague in 1510, and Titian finished some of his unfinished pictures.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: So whose hand is this? Look closely, and do not hurry to a name.

q3.text: Why is it so hard to tell their early work apart?

b3a.text: Yes. Titian formed his early style alongside Giorgione and even completed some of his pictures, so their hands are hard to separate.

b3b.text: No: the problem is their closeness.

correction.truth: The difficulty is their closeness: Titian learned from Giorgione and finished some of his pictures.
correction.evidence: The National Gallery, London; the Louvre.

correction.truth: Their works survive; what is hard is telling them apart, because they worked so closely.
correction.evidence: The National Gallery, London; the Louvre.

n4.text: It belongs to a Venetian tradition: people making music outdoors, in a landscape that matters as much as the figures. Centuries later, it stood behind a famous scandal.

q4.text: Manet's 1863 picnic scene drew on it and caused a scandal. Why?

choices.label: A nude woman sat among clothed men
It was too big for the Salon

b4a.text: The emperor even allowed the show.

correction.truth: Napoleon III allowed the Salon des Refusés. The shock was a nude woman among men in modern clothes.

b4b.text: Yes. Manet put a nude woman between men in modern black coats. Defenders pointed to this picture, then called Giorgione's; critics were not persuaded.

correction.tempting: The official Salon jury turned it away.
correction.truth: It hung in the Salon des Refusés. What shocked was the nude woman among clothed men.

n5.text: Louis XIV bought it in 1671. Long called a Giorgione, now credited to Titian, it still makes people argue about whose hand it is.

lessons.takeaway: Two clothed musicians and two nude women in a landscape: long called a Giorgione, now credited to Titian after centuries of argument, it later stood behind Manet's scandalous picnic.
